_readme: Scout notes for the twenty-first photo batch (Oct 29, 2026), in two parts. Batch 21: the day-5 God-list pages spider-beetles, baby-silverfish and tomato-hornworms. Batch 21b: the day-4 pages lovebugs, wood-roaches, sweat-bees, ground-bees, crazy-ants, skunk-smell-in-house and copperhead-look-alikes, plus two extras the coordinator asked for (false-widow-spiders, woodlouse-spiders). Same format as batches 7 to 20: what each photo's source says it shows and who identified it (sourceDescription), the pages it serves (forPages), confidence in the identification, whether it can lead a page (leadEligible: public domain or CC0 AND a confident identification of the page's main subject), and caveats. Licence, credit and size of record are in photos.json and repeated in note. 45 photos were added: 18 in batch 21 (leads: a smooth spider beetle on a ruler, a pale 7 mm young gray silverfish and a tomato hornworm eating the observer's tomatoes, all CC0) and 27 in batch 21b (leads: a striped skunk on a lawn, CC0, and a juvenile copperhead identified by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, public domain). Every image was opened before choosing and again as the WebP the script wrote. Hornworms were checked against the marks UMN, MSU and Wisconsin give and are captioned only as far as the marks and the identifications agree. Snakes follow the Snakes rule in WRITER_BRIEF_PHOTO_ID.md: all nine snake photos were identified by a government agency (USFWS, USGS, NOAA, NPS) or come from CDC PHIL with a herpetologist's photo; no iNaturalist or Commons community identification was used for a snake. Identifiers named in caveats: szucsich is Nikola Szucsich, by far the most active identifier of silverfish on iNaturalist (about 23,000 silverfish identifications); johnascher is John S. Ascher, a bee systematist and the most prolific bee identifier on iNaturalist; sabutaro is Jiri Hromadka, a very active cockroach identifier (about 245,000 identifications). Searches, refusals and what is still missing are in gaps.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Gibbium aequinoctiale by mnathan and birthedofearth; a third identifier stopped at insect; annotated adult, dead). BugGuide says Gibbium species are reliably separated only by male genitalia, so 'smooth spider beetle (Gibbium)' is the safe caption; G. aequinoctiale is the species the sources report in North America
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 53842740 by dmcmanus (Deaglan McManus), Allison Park, Pennsylvania, May 13, 2020, CC0, no description. Three photos of the same beetle on a ruler with red marks; photo 85649705 used (from above).
candidates.caveats: A sharp top view of a smooth spider beetle on a ruler between its 0 and 1 marks: the shiny, reddish-brown, globe-shaped body on long, pale legs. The ruler's units are not stated; ten divisions between 0 and 1 and a beetle about 2.5 divisions long fit a centimetre ruler in millimetres, but caption it only 'on a ruler, for scale' unless the writer confirms. Annotated dead: do not say it was alive or walking. Where it was found is not stated. CC0 and confidently identified: the lead and share image for spider-beetles.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1149x1229.

candidates.confidence: high at genus (determined by kerbtier.de, a German team of beetle experts, as Gibbium psylloides or G. aequinoctiale shortly after the photo was taken, per the photographer Francisco Welter-Schultes); not identified to species
candidates.sourceDescription: Wikimedia Commons file Gibbium-03-fws.jpg by Francisco Welter-Schultes, CC0, May 31, 2022: 'Gibbium Scopoli, 1777. Body length 2.8 mm without antennae. Determined by kerbtier.de as Gibbium psylloides or aequinoctiale shortly after the picture was taken ... Germany: Bayern, Landkreis Ansbach, Heilsbronn.' One of ten views of the same beetle (Gibbium-01-fws.jpg to Gibbium-10-fws.jpg).
candidates.caveats: A clean studio top view on white: six legs and two long antennae spread around the shiny, reddish-brown, globe-shaped body. The figure for the page's tick test (a beetle's six legs and antennae against a tick's eight legs and none). Genus only: caption 'smooth spider beetle (genus Gibbium)', no species. Photographed in Germany: leave the place out on the US page or say so. 2.8 mm is the photographer's measure. CC0 with an expert determination: could lead too, but the ruler photo is the planned lead. Original 968 px wide.
candidates.note: Credit: Francisco Welter-Schultes, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 968x908.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Gibbium aequinoctiale by the observer ryanfm and by hdspotter); the genus-level caution above applies
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 373348406 by ryanfm (Ryan F. Mandelbaum), 5th Ave, New York, New York, June 19, 2026, CC BY, no description. Three photos; photo 682299339 used.
candidates.caveats: A smooth spider beetle on the tip of a finger beside the nail: the size photo (no spider beetle beside a coin or a tick exists under an allowed licence). Say only that it is on a fingertip; that spider beetles do not bite people must come from the page's sources. Where it was found is not stated. CC BY, so never the lead or share image.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Ryan F. Mandelbaum, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Gibbium aequinoctiale by the observer mertensia and by malisaspring; thebals at genus Gibbium). The observer herself quotes BugGuide: reliable species identification needs male genitalia
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 39777884 by mertensia (Bonnie Semmling), Somerville, New Jersey, March 9, 2020, CC BY: 'Found in shower'. Five photos; photo 63142878 used.
candidates.caveats: Where found: a smooth spider beetle on a metal ledge beside a bar of soap in the shower where the observer found it, tile below. A real household find, not posed. Do not add that moisture or bathrooms attract them unless a source says it. CC BY: below the lead only.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Bonnie Semmling, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade with four identifications on Gibbium aequinoctiale: aurion, pmbrousseau, rguy321 and frontyardscientist; the observer first guessed arachnid and withdrew it); annotated adult, alive
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 105843220 by aurion, Quebec, Canada, January 30, 2022: 'Flea or tick?'. One photo, 177684251, licensed CC0 (the observation record itself is CC BY-NC; the photo's own licence is what the script checks and what the page uses).
candidates.caveats: A live smooth spider beetle walking on white fabric, posted by an observer asking 'Flea or tick?': the confusion the page answers. The source does not say what the fabric is (sheet, clothing or upholstery): do not call it bedding. The beetle is small in a wide frame (1200x540), so it is a where-found photo, not a good lead. Canadian observation: on the US page say Quebec, Canada, or leave the place out. Quote no more than the observer's three words.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x540.

candidates.confidence: high at species (research grade: Ctenolepisma longicaudatum by the observer kenkneidel and by szucsich, Nikola Szucsich). Young by the observer's measure and note, not by annotation
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 10519869 by kenkneidel (Ken Kneidel), Charlotte, North Carolina, March 18, 2018, CC0: 'rear of abdomen has 2 pairs of styli, indoors, small (7mm) but possibly early instar'. Five photos (one whole insect, four close-ups); photo 14640317 used, the whole insect.
candidates.caveats: A sharp view of a pale tan young gray silverfish on a green background (the photographer's backdrop, not where it was found): long antennae, three tail filaments, a body not yet the adult's silvery gray. Found indoors; 7 mm is the observer's measure and 'possibly early instar' the observer's guess: give no age or instar. Adult size and when the scales come must come from the page's sources (UC IPM, NC State). Original 992 px wide. CC0 and confidently identified: the lead and share image for baby-silverfish.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 992x760.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Ctenolepisma longicaudatum by the observer coniver and by mantis777; annotated juvenile, alive)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 291457063 by coniver, Exeter, England, May 31, 2025, CC0, no description. Twelve photos of the same young silverfish on a person's arm and on a speckled surface; photo 524453481 used (beside a fingertip).
candidates.caveats: The size photo: a young gray silverfish on a speckled surface next to a fingertip; the insect is small in the frame, which is the point. The source does not say what the surface is: say 'a speckled surface', not a countertop or kitchen. Photographed in England; the same species lives in US homes, so leave the place out. The frames on skin were not used.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: medium, family only (Lepismatidae: starkowl proposed the common silverfish, Lepisma saccharinum, and highwaytohellgrammite disagreed back to family; needs ID, not research grade); annotated juvenile
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 18943285 by swells (Steve Wells), Holualoa, Hawaii, December 10, 2018, CC0: 'In a book, near the binding'. Two photos; photo 29040956 used.
candidates.caveats: Where found: a pale, bristly young silverfish on a dark, speckled surface that the observer describes as a book near its binding; the book itself is not recognisable in the frame. The species is disputed: caption it 'a young silverfish (family Lepismatidae)' at most, never the common silverfish. Not research grade, so never the lead.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x871.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Thermobia domestica by the observer estv and by szucsich, Nikola Szucsich)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 35413318 by estv (Esteban Gastelum Leyva), Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico, November 7, 2019, CC0, no description. Two photos; photo 55838568 used.
candidates.caveats: A firebrat on a white textured surface (a wall or ceiling texture; the source does not say): mottled, banded back, long antennae and tail filaments. For the firebrat row or card on baby-silverfish and the firebrat media placeholder on /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-silverfish. Life stage not annotated: do not call it a nymph. Photographed in Mexico: leave the place out or say Sonora, Mexico. CC0 and confidently identified, but not either page's main subject, so not a lead.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade, four identifiers agreeing on Manduca quinquemaculatus: the observer mcm, carolinashepherd, hughmcguinness and k8thegr8; annotated larva). Marks checked at full size: V-shaped white marks with a spiracle inside each V and a dark blue-black horn
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 12730966 by mcm (Mike Mullins), Sweeny, Texas, May 22, 2018, CC0: 'Eating my tomatoes !!!'. One photo, 18439767.
candidates.caveats: A tomato hornworm lying along a tomato stem among tomato leaves, a planter and deck boards behind: the lead and share image for tomato-hornworms. The caterpillar fills the upper part of a tall frame; the V marks and the dark horn are clear at full size. No size given. Identifications and marks agree, so the species can be captioned with confidence.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade, six identifiers on Manduca quinquemaculatus: sgalick, schoenitz, hughmcguinness, colinpurrington, carolinashepherd and mia130; annotated larva). Marks checked: clear V-shaped marks with a spiracle in each V, dark horn
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 7206501 by sgalick (Samuel Paul Galick), Middle Township, New Jersey, July 7, 2017, no description. One photo, 9296602, licensed CC0 (the observation record is CC BY).
candidates.caveats: A tomato hornworm hanging under a hairy tomato stem, backlit, with garden twine across the frame: the clearest view of the V marks, for the side-by-side with the tobacco hornworm. A little dark and shadowed. CC0.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Manduca sexta by the observer danieldas and by b_dvorak, one of the two most active Manduca identifiers on iNaturalist). Marks checked: diagonal white lines edged in black above and a reddish horn
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 402877548 by danieldas (Daniel Das), California, September 21, 2026, CC0: 'On tomato plant'. Six photos; photo 739638997 used (side view with the horn).
candidates.caveats: A tobacco hornworm on a tomato stem: the diagonal white lines with black upper edges and the reddish, curved horn. The comparison photo for the side-by-side (the tobacco hornworm is just as common on tomatoes). CC0 and confidently identified, but the page's main subject is the tomato hornworm, so it does not lead.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x900.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Manduca sexta by the observer jacob_mullin and by claire97357). Marks checked: diagonal lines edged in black and a red horn, so a tobacco hornworm
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 389067186 by jacob_mullin (Jacob Mullin), Groton, Massachusetts, August 7, 2026, CC0: 'Saw tons of it's droppings below the tomato plant this morning. I had no idea what I was looking at until I spotted this caterpillar up top.' Four photos; photo 712627500 used.
candidates.caveats: Where found and the damage: a tobacco hornworm stretched along the top of a potted tomato plant whose upper stems are stripped bare, house siding, windows, a wall clock and a covered grill behind (no brand legible; checked at full size). The droppings the observer mentions are not in this photo. Caption as a tobacco hornworm, or as 'a hornworm' in a damage caption.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Manduca sexta by the observer kevin-anderson and by toriw; annotated larva). Marks checked: diagonal lines edged in black, red horn
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 384685423 by kevin-anderson (Kevin Anderson), Durham, North Carolina, July 24, 2026, CC BY: 'Munching our tomatoes'. One photo, 704197775.
candidates.caveats: The damage to fruit: a tobacco hornworm on a tomato stem just below a green tomato with a large bite out of it, lattice behind. The photo does not show this caterpillar making that bite; the observer says it was munching their tomatoes, so 'a hornworm beside a green tomato it has been eating' is at the source's strength. No frass visible. CC BY: never the lead.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Kevin Anderson, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x1200.

candidates.confidence: high for the wasp (research grade: Cotesia congregata by the observer birdnirdfoley and by mmn_noriko); the host hornworm is not identified (its horn looks reddish, which would point to a tobacco hornworm)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 178906087 by birdnirdfoley, Smithsburg, Maryland, August 17, 2023, CC0, no description. One photo, 311393552.
candidates.caveats: A hornworm on a tomato stem beside green tomatoes, its back covered in dozens of white silk cocoons: the 'leave it' photo. Caption the host only as 'a hornworm'. The observation is of the wasp. Call them cocoons, not eggs; the advice to leave parasitized hornworms must come from the extension sources (UMN, Maine, UF/IFAS), not the photo. CC0.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x900.

candidates.confidence: medium-high (the photographer's identification as droppings of a Manduca sexta larva; no second identification, but the barrel-shaped, ridged pellets fit hornworm frass, and the photo is not used to identify the caterpillar)
candidates.sourceDescription: Wikimedia Commons file 'Manduca sexta droppings.png' by ButterNoodle, CC BY-SA 4.0: 'Droppings from a Manduca sexta larva'. No place or date given.
candidates.caveats: About 35 dark green, barrel-shaped, ridged pellets on white paper: what hornworm frass looks like close up, the sign the page says gives them away. Probably from a reared caterpillar; the source does not say. Caption as 'droppings (frass) of a tobacco hornworm, as the photographer identifies them' or simply 'hornworm droppings'. CC BY-SA: credit as recorded, never the lead.
candidates.note: Credit: ButterNoodle, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC-BY-SA-4.0. Size: 1200x791.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Manduca quinquemaculatus by the observer aaron_pritchard and by stomlins701, the most active Manduca identifier on iNaturalist; annotated adult, alive)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 378417098 by aaron_pritchard, Harlan, Iowa, September 15, 2018, CC0, no description. Seven photos; photo 692094101 used.
candidates.caveats: The adult tomato hornworm moth, wings spread flat on a gray surface: gray-brown wing pattern and the yellow-orange spots along the abdomen. Not every spot pair is visible from this angle, so take the count (five pairs; six in the Carolina sphinx) from the sources, not the photo. The place on record is a hospital heliport in Harlan: say Iowa or leave it out. CC0; a life-stage photo, not the page's lead.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x675.

candidates.confidence: high at genus, medium at species (research grade: Manduca sexta by the observer peterboyer and by zoology123, but a pupa alone is hard to tell from the tomato hornworm's; annotated pupa)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 10253531 by peterboyer (Peter Boyer), Wooster, Ohio, March 17, 2017, CC BY, no description. One photo, 14185074.
candidates.caveats: A reddish-brown hornworm pupa with the looped 'handle' along its front, lying in its cell in the soil, photographed in March: the overwintering stage the page describes. Caption it 'a hornworm pupa in the soil'; name the tobacco hornworm only as 'identified on iNaturalist as'. The source does not say how it was found. CC BY.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Peter Boyer, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x900.

candidates.confidence: high for the observation (research grade: Plecia nearctica by the observer buggybuddy, zdanko and mecopteron_bouillon); in this wide frame the splattered insects are too small to identify on their own, so the identification rests on the observation and its close-ups
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 113299076 by buggybuddy (Jade Fortnash), Pembroke Pines, Florida, April 28, 2022, CC0, no description. Three photos of squashed lovebugs on a vehicle; photo 191441994 used (the front of the vehicle).
candidates.caveats: The photo the reader needs: lovebugs splattered across the chrome grille, a white trim panel and the gray bumper of a vehicle, a headlight at left. The source does not say what kind of vehicle or where it was driven: say 'a vehicle', not a truck or a car on a highway. Any claim about lovebug splatter damaging paint must come from the page's sources (UF/IFAS), not the photo. CC0, but not a lead: the insects are specks at this distance.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x900.

candidates.confidence: high (same research-grade observation as lovebugs-splattered-vehicle-grille; the orange thorax and black wings are visible on the squashed bodies)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 113299076 by buggybuddy (Jade Fortnash), Pembroke Pines, Florida, April 28, 2022, CC0, no description; photo 191441951 used.
candidates.caveats: A close-up of three or four squashed lovebugs and their smeared remains on a white painted surface, flecked with other insect bits. Pairs with the grille photo to show what the splatter is. The source does not say which part of the vehicle this is: 'on a white painted surface'.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Plecia nearctica by bruceneville, mecopteron_bouillon and the observer mbelitz, who first put it at genus)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 33073256 by mbelitz (Michael W Belitz), Hawthorne, Florida, September 20, 2019, CC0, no description. Photo 51915155 used.
candidates.caveats: About twenty live lovebugs, several joined tail to tail in pairs, crowded on a blue surface: the swarm the page describes, close up. The source does not say what the blue surface is (it may be a vehicle, a tarp or a wall): do not name it. The pairs are visible, but say 'in mating pairs' only where the page's sources describe the paired flight. CC0 and confidently identified, so it could lead, though the mating-pair lead already on record is planned.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Plecia nearctica by sam10turner, zdanko and the observer erickalee, who first put it at genus)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 115761150 by erickalee, Simonton, Texas, May 6, 2022, CC0, no description. Photo 195375517 used.
candidates.caveats: The size photo: a single lovebug standing on a fingernail, its orange thorax, black body and wings clear. Lovebugs do not bite or sting, but say so only from the page's sources. Original 942 px wide.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 942x1256.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Parcoblatta pennsylvanica by the observer vrose96 and by sabutaro, Jiri Hromadka; annotated adult, female, alive, with egg evidence)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 286671153 by vrose96, Gordo, Alabama (the record's place is 'Gordo'; its coordinates put it in Pickens County, Alabama), June 3, 2025, CC0, no description. Two photos; photo 515385222 used.
candidates.caveats: The sex difference the page needs: an adult female Pennsylvania wood cockroach, dark and broad, with short wings that leave most of the abdomen bare, carrying a pale egg case (ootheca) at the tip of her abdomen, on leaf litter and gravel. 'Short wings' is what the photo shows; the rule that females of this species are short-winged and do not fly must come from the page's sources. CC0 and confidently identified: a stronger lead than wood-cockroach-male, which is already a figure on /blog/can-cockroaches-fly.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Parcoblatta pennsylvanica by the observer conhawn and by sabutaro, Jiri Hromadka)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 222157840 by conhawn (Conway Hawn), Missouri (the record's place reads 'Sherrill Township, MO'), June 11, 2024, CC0, no description. Two photos; photo 393498287 used.
candidates.caveats: Where found: a long-winged adult (wings covering the abdomen; not sexed on the record, but long wings fit a male) on white horizontal siding, lit by the camera's flash. The source does not say it was a house or that it was night: the siding and the hard flash shadow are what the photo shows. Say 'on white siding'.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1331.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Parcoblatta pennsylvanica by the observer jdonahue and by sabutaro, Jiri Hromadka)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 219227824 by jdonahue (Justin Donahue), D.H. Day Campground, Empire, Michigan, May 28, 2024, CC BY: 'found indoors, deceased'. Two photos; photo 388428779 used.
candidates.caveats: Where found, the reader's own situation: a wood cockroach the observer found dead indoors, photographed on a paper towel. The record is at a campground, so the building is probably not a house: say 'found indoors', not 'in a home'. Dead: do not say it was alive or wandering. CC BY, so never the lead.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Justin Donahue, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high to subgenus (research grade at Lasioglossum subgenus Dialictus: the observer swells and johnascher, John S. Ascher); not identified to species, as usual for Dialictus from photos
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 45422279 by swells (Steve Wells), Moscow, Idaho, May 9, 2020, CC0: 'This little guy landed on and didn't want to leave my wife's finger.' Three photos; photo 72023903 used.
candidates.caveats: The photo the reader needs, a sweat bee on skin: a small, dark, faintly metallic bee standing on a fingertip, wings folded. It also covers the wished-for 'small dark Lasioglossum'. The source does not say it was drinking sweat: do not caption it as drinking; that sweat bees are drawn to perspiration must come from the page's sources. Caption the bee as 'a sweat bee (Lasioglossum, subgenus Dialictus)'. CC0 with an expert identification, so it could lead instead of the green Augochlora on record.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1211.

candidates.confidence: high for the bee (research grade: Lasioglossum zephyrus by klittle2 and johnascher, John S. Ascher; the observer put it at Dialictus); the nest is linked to that bee only by the observer's note
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 80513150 by kenkneidel (Ken Kneidel), Charlotte, North Carolina, May 21, 2021, CC0: '6 to 7 mm, solitary with cone of dirt grains around entrance hole (see last photo)'. Eight photos: seven of the bee (annotated adult, female, dead) on white, and the nest; photo 131969024 used (the nest).
candidates.caveats: A sweat bee nest: a small round entrance hole in the middle of a neat cone of loose soil grains on bare, gravelly ground. No bee in the frame. Caption it as 'the nest entrance of a sweat bee (Lasioglossum zephyrus, per the observation)'. Also a card-quality comparison for ground-bees (a sweat bee's tiny mound beside a mining bee's), if that page wants it. Not a lead.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1042.

candidates.confidence: high at genus, medium-high at species (research grade: Andrena barbara by jordan_kue and hsteig; the observer, hurlbert, says genus Andrena). Species-level identification of Andrena from a photo is often tentative: genus is the safe caption
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 264940777 by hurlbert (Allen Hurlbert), University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill campus, March 11, 2025, CC0: 'Emergence now extends along north slope to Coker main entrance. Thousands to tens of thousands, but north slope emergence has not yet peaked.' Two photos; photo 475804686 used.
candidates.caveats: Where found, live: a mining bee on bare red clay a few centimeters from an open burrow, grass blades around, at a campus nesting aggregation the observer counts in the thousands (his other observations there call it a lawn and a slope). Caption 'a mining bee (genus Andrena) beside a nest burrow'. Not a wide shot of the aggregation. CC0: a better lead than the museum specimen mining-bee.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1600.

candidates.confidence: high (research grade: Paratrechina longicornis by the observer buster7 and by pioneer_entomology)
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist observation 238663273 by buster7 (Buster Crow), Kingsville, Texas, August 29, 2024, CC0, no description. One photo, 424930938.
candidates.caveats: A dense mass of longhorn crazy ants, hundreds of workers, many carrying white brood, streaming over a painted vertical surface (a post, frame or wall; the source does not say). The 'mass' photo the page wanted, though of longhorn rather than tawny crazy ants: caption the species accordingly. Do not say the colony was moving house unless a source says brood carrying means that. Tall narrow frame (945x2048).

The tail tip is pale yellow-green in this photo: write 'yellow or greenish-yellow tail tip' at the agencies' strength. 1024x768 original; fine at article width. Public domain and agency-identified: lead and share image. Also unblocks the held baby-snakes page.
